In Apple's fiscal 2024 Form 10-K (FY ended September 28, 2024), four reported results for FY2024 vs. FY2023 were described as unfavorably affected by the weakness of foreign currencies against the U.S. dollar:

**1. Greater China segment net sales** — "The weakness in the **renminbi** relative to the U.S. dollar had an unfavorable year-over-year impact on Greater China net sales during 2024." (Segment sales fell 8% to $66,952M, primarily due to lower iPhone and iPad net sales, with currency weakness an additional adverse factor.)

**2. Japan segment net sales** — "The weakness in the **yen** relative to the U.S. dollar had an unfavorable year-over-year impact on Japan net sales during 2024." (Segment sales rose 3% to $25,052M, primarily from higher iPhone net sales, but currency was an offsetting drag.)

**3. Rest of Asia Pacific segment net sales** — "The weakness in foreign currencies relative to the U.S. dollar had a net unfavorable year-over-year impact on Rest of Asia Pacific net sales during 2024." (Segment sales rose 4% to $30,658M, primarily from higher Services net sales.)

**4. Products gross margin (and Products gross margin percentage)** — Products gross margin and gross margin percentage increased in 2024 vs. 2023 "due to cost savings, partially offset by a different Products mix and the **weakness in foreign currencies** relative to the U.S. dollar." (Products gross margin rose to $109,633M, or 37.2% of sales, from $108,803M, or 36.5%.)

### Notes / what was not affected
- **Services gross margin** and **Services gross margin percentage** were attributed to higher Services net sales and a different Services mix — not currency weakness.
- **Operating expenses** (R&D +5%, SG&A +5%) were attributed to headcount-related costs and general expense growth, not currencies.
- **The effective tax rate** (24.1% in 2024 vs. 14.7% in 2023) was attributed to the $10.2 billion State Aid Decision charge, state taxes, higher foreign earnings rates, and lower share-based compensation benefits — not currency weakness.
- **Item 7A (Market Risk)** states generally that "a strengthening of the U.S. dollar will negatively affect the Company's net sales and gross margins as expressed in U.S. dollars," and that Apple may choose not to hedge certain exposures, but this is a forward-looking/general risk disclosure rather than a fiscal 2024 result.
- No currency-related comment is made for **Americas** or **Europe** segment net sales, nor for any product-category net sales line (iPhone, Mac, iPad, Wearables/Home/Accessories, Services).

## NVIDIA FY2024 Form 10-K — Inventory and Excess Purchase Commitment Charges to Cost of Revenue (FY ended January 28, 2024)

**1. Total charges — $2.2 billion (MD&A, Item 7 "Gross Profit and Gross Margin," p. 40)**

> "Provisions for inventory and excess inventory purchase obligations totaled $2.2 billion for both fiscal years 2024 and 2023."

The $2.2 billion is broken into two separately disclosed components, both charged to cost of revenue:

| Component | FY2024 Amount | Source | What it represents |
|---|---|---|---|
| Inventory provision (write-down of inventory) | **$774 million** | Note 10 (Balance Sheet Components), footnote (1) to Inventories, p. 68 | Write-down of inventory to the lower of cost or net realizable value, i.e. excess or obsolete inventory |
| Expense for inventory purchase obligations in excess of demand | **approximately $1.4 billion** | Note 10, footnote (1) to Accrued and Other Current Liabilities, p. 70 | "inventory purchase obligations in excess of our current demand projections, supplier charges and for penalties related to cancellations and underutilization" |

Note the two components sum to the disclosed $2.2 billion total ($774 million + ~$1.4 billion).

**2. Provision release — $540 million (MD&A, p. 40)**

> "Sales of previously reserved inventory or settlements of excess inventory purchase obligations resulted in a provision release of $540 million ... for fiscal years 2024."

This is a credit to cost of revenue arising from (a) selling inventory that had already been written down and (b) settling excess inventory purchase obligations for amounts below the amount previously accrued.

**3. Net effect (arithmetic, not a separately stated figure)**

Approximately **$1.7 billion** net ($2.2 billion of provisions less $540 million of releases) was charged to cost of revenue in fiscal 2024 on these items.

**Supporting context in the filing**

- **Policy (Note 1, Inventories, p. 58):** NVIDIA "charge[s] cost of sales for inventory provisions to write-down our inventory to the lower of cost or net realizable value or for obsolete or excess inventory, and for excess product purchase commitments," and "we record a liability for noncancelable purchase commitments with suppliers for quantities in excess of our future demand forecasts consistent with our valuation of obsolete or excess inventory." Once written down, inventory establishes a new cost basis that "is not subsequently written up."
- **PwC Critical Audit Matter (p. 49):** "Valuation of Inventories — Provisions for Excess or Obsolete Inventories and Excess Product Purchase Commitments," referencing Notes 1, 10 and 13. This confirms the amounts above as the audited subject matter; the $5.3 billion inventory balance and $16.1 billion of inventory purchase and long-term supply/capacity obligations it cites are year-end balances and are excluded per your instruction.
- **Driver (MD&A, p. 36 and p. 40):** gross margin improved "primarily due to strong Data Center revenue growth of 217% and lower net inventory provisions as a percentage of revenue."

**Excluded as instructed:** year-end balances (total inventories $5,282 million; excess inventory purchase obligations accrued $1,655 million; inventory purchase and long-term supply/capacity obligations $16.1 billion), gross margin percentage impacts (2.7% unfavorable net effect; 72.7% gross margin), and all fiscal 2023 comparatives.

## Walmart fiscal 2026 Form 10-K (FY ended January 31, 2026) — cross-currency swaps

**Source: WMT_2026_10K.pdf, Note 7 "Fair Value Measurements" (p. 69), Note 1 "Derivatives — Cash Flow Hedges" (p. 61), and Item 7A "Foreign Currency Risk" (p. 47).**

### The two dollar amounts as of January 31, 2026

| Measure | Amount as stated | What it represents |
|---|---|---|
| Notional amount | **$6,020 million** (i.e., $6.02 billion) | The aggregate face/notional principal amount of the receive fixed-rate, pay fixed-rate cross-currency swaps designated as cash flow hedges. Notional is used to compute the contractual cash flows to be exchanged under the contracts. |
| Fair value | **$(920) million** (a liability of $0.9 billion) | The estimated amount the Company would pay upon termination of the swap agreements as of January 31, 2026 (Level 2 fair value, income approach using interest rate and foreign currency forward curves). Classified primarily in "deferred income taxes and other" in the Consolidated Balance Sheets. |

Item 7A states the same position in rounded terms: "The aggregate fair value of these swaps was in a liability position of $0.9 billion … as of January 31, 2026." The change in fair value was attributed to fluctuations in currency exchange rates, primarily from the strengthening of certain currencies relative to the U.S. dollar in fiscal 2026.

### What these swaps do (per Note 1, p. 61)

Walmart is a party to **receive fixed-rate, pay fixed-rate cross-currency interest rate swaps** used to hedge the currency exposure associated with the **forecasted payments of principal and interest of certain non-U.S. denominated debt**. Changes in fair value are recorded in **accumulated other comprehensive loss** and subsequently reclassified into earnings in the period the hedged forecasted transaction affects earnings. These derivatives **mature on dates ranging from April 2026 to January 2039**.

### Related sensitivity disclosures (Item 7A, p. 47)

- A hypothetical uniform **10% weakening** of the U.S. dollar against the other currencies underlying these swaps would have changed their value by **$0.7 billion**.
- A hypothetical **10% change in interest rates** underlying these swaps from rates in effect at January 31, 2026 would have changed their value by **$0.1 billion**.

*(As requested, January 31, 2025 comparatives ($5,452 million notional; $1,388 million fair value), amounts reclassified out of accumulated other comprehensive loss, and the receive fixed-rate/pay variable-rate interest rate swap figures have been excluded.)*

**$15.6 billion increase, entirely allocated to the Compute & Networking reporting unit** (Note 5, p. 63). This is the bridge from the prior-year balance to the $20.8 billion year-end balance.

Cash flow shows "Groq, Inc." $13,000M in investing activities. Pro forma results were not presented as the effect was immaterial.

The remaining roughly **$1.2 billion** of the $15.6 billion increase (i.e., $15.6B less the $14.4B Groq goodwill) is not separately quantified; it relates to NVIDIA's other fiscal 2026 acquisitions (cash flow shows "Acquisitions, net of cash acquired" of $1,535M, and the equity statement records $28M of fair value of partially vested equity awards assumed in connection with acquisitions).

The prior-year balance at January 26, 2025 ($5,188M total, comprising $4.8B in Compute & Networking and $370M in Graphics) is excluded above except where used only as the starting point for the $15.6B fiscal 2026 increase.

Reading Item 3 (Legal Proceedings) and Item 1A (Risk Factors) of Apple's fiscal 2025 Form 10-K (fiscal year ended September 27, 2025; filed October 31, 2025), the filing dates four developments to a specific day or month of calendar year 2025:

### 1. April 23, 2025 — EU Digital Markets Act (two actions)

**Article 5(4) Investigation (steering/anti-steering):** The European Commission fined Apple **€500 million** and issued a **cease and desist order** requiring Apple to remove the technical and commercial restrictions that prevent developers from steering users to alternative distribution channels outside the App Store. Apple has appealed the Commission's Article 5(4) decision.

**Article 6(4) Investigation (new developer contract terms):** Also on April 23, 2025, the Commission issued **preliminary findings** that Apple's new contractual requirements for third-party app developers and app marketplaces may violate the DMA. If the Commission makes a final violation determination, it can issue a cease and desist order and impose fines of **up to 10% of Apple's annual worldwide net sales**; it may also impose additional fines for violating a cease and desist order. Apple says it believes it complies and has continued revising its DMA compliance plan in response to Commission feedback.

### 2. April 30, 2025 — Epic Games (N.D. Cal.)

The California District Court (Northern District of California) **found Apple in violation of the 2021 Injunction** and enjoined Apple from:
- imposing any commission or fee on purchases consumers make outside an app;
- restricting, conditioning, limiting or prohibiting how developers guide consumers to purchases outside an app; and
- otherwise interfering with a consumer's choice to proceed in or out of an app.

The court also **denied Apple's motion to narrow or vacate the 2021 Injunction** and **referred Apple to the U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of California** to determine whether criminal contempt proceedings are appropriate. Apple appealed to the Ninth Circuit.

### 3. September 2, 2025 — Google search remedies (D.C. District Court)

This matter involves a company with which Apple has a commercial relationship (Apple earns revenue from Google search-licensing arrangements). Following the **August 5, 2024** finding that Google violated U.S. antitrust laws, the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia **ordered certain remedies on September 2, 2025**. The order is subject to further proceedings before that court (which may change its interpretation or application, or order new/changed remedies) and to appeal by both the DOJ and Google. The filing notes that a reversal on appeal could result in DOJ's initially proposed remedies being imposed, such as those prohibiting Google from offering Apple commercial terms for search distribution — which could materially affect Apple's licensing revenue.

### 4. October 2025 — Ninth Circuit oral argument in Epic Games

After Apple's **request to stay the April 30, 2025 decision pending appeal was denied**, the Ninth Circuit Court agreed to hear Apple's appeal on an expedited basis, with **oral arguments heard in October 2025**.

### Related item dated only to a period, not a specific day/month
Under "Other Legal Proceedings," the filing states that Apple **settled certain matters during the fourth quarter of 2025** that did not individually or in the aggregate have a material impact on its financial condition or operating results. This is a fiscal-quarter reference rather than a specific 2025 date.

**Not dated to 2025 (for context):** the DMA Article 5(4) investigation opened March 25, 2024; the Article 6(4) investigation opened June 24, 2024; the DOJ/state antitrust lawsuit was filed March 21, 2024; the 2021 Epic injunction was entered in 2021; and Apple's compliance plan was implemented January 16, 2024 with its motion to narrow the injunction filed September 30, 2024.

## Where the figures come from

Pfizer's 2025 Form 10-K, Note 10 (Identifiable Intangible Assets, Net and Goodwill), shows the IPR&D line (an indefinite-lived asset) with a gross carrying amount of **$21,760 million at December 31, 2025 vs. $18,893 million at December 31, 2024** — an increase of roughly $2.9 billion. The 10-K does not present a full rollforward table for IPR&D; the drivers are explained in the footnotes to the table and in the supporting notes.

## Causes of the increase

**1. The Metsera acquisition (the dominant driver).** On November 13, 2025 Pfizer acquired Metsera, a clinical-stage company in obesity and cardiometabolic disease, for $65.60 per share in cash plus a CVR of up to $20.65 per share (up to $2.3 billion of milestone-contingent payments). Total fair value of consideration transferred was **$8.0 billion** ($7.8 billion net of cash acquired), including $632 million for the non-cash CVRs and $475 million for pre-acquisition employee stock awards. In connection with the business combination Pfizer provisionally recorded **$8.0 billion of identifiable intangible assets, net, consisting of IPR&D** (the MET-097i monotherapy and the MET-097i + MET-233i combination), plus $2.2 billion of goodwill, $1.7 billion of net deferred tax liabilities and a $635 million contingent consideration liability. The purchase price allocation was **not yet finalized** and remains subject to significant change. This $8.0 billion IPR&D addition is the principal reason IPR&D grew.

**2. Foreign exchange.** The note states that the increase in gross carrying amounts also reflects the impact of foreign exchange (a modest net effect on the IPR&D line).

## Offsets to the increase

**a. Reclassifications out of IPR&D into developed technology rights.** Upon approval in a major market, Pfizer reclassifies IPR&D assets to finite-lived assets and begins amortizing them. In 2025, **$600 million (Padcev) and $590 million (talazoparib/Talzenna), a total of $1.19 billion, were transferred from IPR&D to developed technology rights**, reducing the IPR&D balance without any cash or earnings effect.

**b. Impairment charges.** 2025 IPR&D impairments of **$3.9 billion** (specifically $3,903 million) reduced the gross carrying amount. Note 4 explains that the 2025 "Certain asset impairments" of **$4,940 million** (up from $3,295 million in 2024) were all attributable to the Biopharma segment and were **"primarily due to changes in development plans and updated long-range commercial forecasts,"** consisting of:
- **$3.9 billion of IPR&D impairments**, primarily including **$1.6 billion for disitamab vedotin, $820 million for Tukysa (tucatinib) and $820 million for osivelotor**; and
- **$1.0 billion of impairments primarily for certain U.S. sterile injectable and hospital products**.

The remaining $1.0 billion of 2025 intangible impairments (outside IPR&D) was $560 million of developed technology rights, $240 million of a finite-lived brand, $210 million of an indefinite-lived licensing agreement and $27 million of a finite-lived licensing agreement.

Supporting program developments described elsewhere in the 10-K bear on those development plans and forecasts: for **osivelotor**, the FDA issued a partial clinical hold in December 2024 and in 2025 concluded that study initiation and enrollment could proceed outside sub-Saharan Africa, with new enrollment expected to begin in the first quarter of 2026; the **Tukysa** 1L/2L/3L HER2+ metastatic breast cancer expansion was removed from Pfizer's late-stage development table; and Pfizer withdrew the sasanlimab filing in the U.S. in December 2025 (EU in February 2026) to allow more time for data collection. Note 4 does not, however, attribute a separate specific cause to each of the three named IPR&D write-downs beyond the general drivers above.

## How the impairment amounts were measured

Per Note 4, the impaired assets were written down to fair value using the income approach — specifically the multi-period excess earnings method (discounted cash flow): forecast expected net cash flows, then apply an asset-specific discount rate. Key assumptions cited are the amount and timing of projected net cash flows (including expected competitive, legal and regulatory effects), the **probability of technical and regulatory success (PTRS)** for ongoing trials, the discount rate, and the tax rate reflecting geographic diversity. All impaired IPR&D was classified as Level 3 (remaining fair value of $4.4 billion). MD&A's critical accounting estimates section adds that IPR&D assets (approximately $21.8 billion at December 31, 2025) are the assets most at risk of impairment, given the uncertain nature of R&D, and lists impairment indicators including adverse changes in legal or business climate, FDA or other regulatory restrictions or withdrawals, expected losses or reduced profits, competitor introductions, changes in development plans or de-prioritization of assets, and clinical trial data or launch-delay changes.

## One item that did *not* affect IPR&D

Pfizer's 2025 in-licensing deals — **3SBio ($1.25 billion upfront, plus a $100 million China option payment, with a $1.35 billion charge recorded in Acquired in-process R&D expenses in Q3 2025)** and **YaoPharma ($150 million upfront)** — were **expensed** rather than capitalized as intangible assets, because the assets had not yet been approved. They therefore increased acquired IPR&D expense, not the IPR&D carrying amount. Likewise, milestone payments under the Abingworth and Blackstone R&D funding arrangements will be recorded as intangible assets when approval-based or sales-based milestones are earned, which did not occur in 2025.

## Effect on reported results

The impairments are recorded in Other (income)/deductions—net. MD&A attributes the $2.3 billion unfavorable year-over-year change in that line primarily to **higher intangible asset impairments of $1.6 billion**, alongside net losses on equity securities versus prior-year gains, the non-recurrence of the 2024 Haleon sale gains, and higher legal charges. In the non-GAAP reconciliation, the full $4,940 million of certain asset impairments is excluded as a "Certain Significant Item" (versus $3,295 million in 2024), and "Amortization of intangible assets" in 2025 was $4,874 million (down $413 million from $5,286 million, driven by lower amortization on Prevnar, fully amortized assets and prior-year impairments).

## Boeing's 2024 Form 10-K (BA_2024_10K.pdf) — Causes Given for Lower 2024 Commercial Airplane Deliveries

**Context in the filing:** Commercial Airplanes (BCA) deliveries fell from **528 aircraft in 2023 to 348 in 2024** (737: 396 → 265; 787: 73 → 51; 767: 32 → 18; 777: 26 → 14; 747: 1 → 0), and BCA revenues fell $11.0 billion, "primarily due to lower deliveries across all programs and 737-9 customer considerations related to the January 2024 grounding" (Item 7, pp. 26, 28, 35).

### Causes the 10-K links to deliveries

**1. The Alaska Airlines 737-9 accident and the resulting FAA action on quality, inspections and production**
The January 5, 2024 door-plug accident triggered the FAA grounding of ~220 in-service 737-9s, an FAA investigation of the 737 quality control system (including Spirit), and findings that Boeing and Spirit "failed to comply with manufacturing quality control requirements." Delivery-linked effects: all 737-9 aircraft in production had to undergo the FAA-approved enhanced inspection process "prior to delivery"; the FAA said it would not approve rate increases above 38/month or new production lines until Boeing complied; and under its safety and quality plan Boeing "slowed production rates and delayed planned production rate increases." The filing states these actions "significantly impacted our financial position, results of operations and cash flows during 2024" (pp. 6, 9, 26, 37–38).

**2. The IAM District 751 work stoppage**
The contract expired September 12, 2024; 96% of members voted to strike and production of the 737, 767, 777 and 777X (plus KC-46A and P-8A) was halted until the new contract was ratified November 4, 2024, with production resuming in December. The filing states directly: **"The IAM 751 work stoppage significantly reduced aircraft deliveries in the second half of 2024."** (pp. 4, 11, 26, 38)

**3. Certification and entry-into-service delays for new models**
- **737-7 and 737-10:** certification is still pending, including the engine anti-ice engineering solution; ~35 aircraft sat in inventory undelivered at year-end. "The production slow-down, the IAM 751 work stoppage and new agreement, and the timing of minor model certifications have had an adverse impact on our financial position, results of operations and cash flows during 2024" (p. 38).
- **777X:** flight-test delays and revised certification timelines pushed first 777-9 delivery to 2026 and 777-8F to 2028; Boeing also "decided to slow the production rate ramp of 777X," which resulted in "further customer delivery delays" (p. 39).

**4. Supply chain disruption, labor instability and production quality issues (787 and 767 especially)**
The 787 program was slowed "to below 5 per month due to supply chain constraints as well as other production issues." The 767 suffered "factory disruption, including supply chain delays and quality issues," prompting Boeing to slow production to "reduce traveled work and enable supply chain recovery." MD&A also notes that supply chain disruptions from production quality issues, global supply chain constraints and labor instability "have reduced overall productivity" (pp. 27, 38, 39).

**5. Business class seat delays on the 787**
"Delays associated with business class seats adversely impacted 2024 deliveries and will continue to impact deliveries in 2025." (p. 39)

**6. Aircraft built but held in inventory for later delivery (timing shift into 2025)**
~55 pre-2023-built 737-8 aircraft (including ~40 for Chinese customers) plus ~25 pre-2023-built 787 aircraft requiring rework were in inventory at year-end and expected to be delivered in 2025 (pp. 38–39).

### Explicitly excluded (causes given only for rates, costs or revenue, not deliveries)
The 777X and 767 reach-forward losses ($4,079 million combined), abnormal production costs ($1,271 million lower than 2023, including $256 million of 787 rework costs), lower margins, higher R&D, the $443 million of 737-9 customer considerations (a revenue reduction), the IAM 751 pay increases and non-union pay enhancements, and inflation/interest-rate effects. These are described as margin, cost, expense or revenue drivers rather than as causes of fewer deliveries.

### Summary count
**Six delivery-linked causes** (or five if the inventory-timing item is folded into production/supply chain): the 737-9 accident response and FAA-imposed production/inspection constraints; the IAM 751 strike; 737-7/-10 and 777X certification delays; supply chain/quality/labor disruptions (principally 787 and 767); 787 business class seat delays; and the holding of built aircraft in inventory for 2025 delivery.

## The primary driver: net income adjusted for non-cash items

Net income from continuing operations before allocation to noncontrolling interests rose from $2,172 million in 2023 to $8,051 million in 2024, and the non-cash add-backs were roughly stable-to-higher, so the "income adjusted for non-cash items" line rose by about $4.9 billion (from ~$10.9 billion to ~$15.8 billion). - **Lower Cost of sales (−$7.1 billion, or −28%)**, driven mainly by the **non-recurrence of the $6.2 billion non-cash 2023 charge for inventory write-offs and related charges on Paxlovid ($5.0 billion) and Comirnaty ($1.2 billion)**, plus a $2.6 billion favorable sales-mix effect (mainly lower Comirnaty sales); this was partially offset by **$1.9 billion of Seagen-related cost of sales, inclusive of amortization of the acquisition-accounting fair value step-up of inventory**.
- **Higher revenues (+$4.1 billion, +7%, to $63.6 billion)** — Paxlovid (including the favorable $771 million final adjustment of the $3.5 billion non-cash 2023 revenue reversal and $442 million of one-time deliveries to the U.S. SNS), a full year of legacy Seagen revenues, and growth in the Vyndaqel family and Eliquis, partly offset by Comirnaty declines and $349 million of unfavorable FX.
- **Lower restructuring charges and certain acquisition-related costs.**
- Offsetting in earnings: **higher net interest expense ($2.0 billion)**, **higher amortization of intangibles ($553 million)**, **net periodic benefit costs in 2024 versus net periodic benefit credits in 2023 ($760 million)**, and **lower net gains on equity securities ($580 million)**; the cash-flow statement correspondingly shows no COVID-19 inventory write-off add-back in 2024 ($0) versus $6,199 million in 2023, and higher asset write-offs/impairments ($4,242 million vs. $3,408 million).

## Offsetting factor 1: decrease in advance payments for Comirnaty and Paxlovid

Paxlovid and Comirnaty deferred revenues fell from **$5.1 billion at year-end 2023 to $2.2 billion at year-end 2024** (Note 17C), because cash collected as advances in prior years was recognized in 2024 revenue as products were delivered (about $2.9 billion of the prior-year balance was recognized in 2024, including the $442 million SNS delivery and the $771 million favorable Paxlovid adjustment), partially offset by new advance payments under amended contracts. Because the cash was received in an earlier period, this is a use (not a source) of 2024 operating cash flow and is visible largely in the "Other liabilities" change (−$3,115 million in 2024 vs. +$595 million in 2023).

## Offsetting factor 2: net changes in inventory greater than one year — the cause Pfizer gives

Per **Note 8A (Inventories)** and the **Note 1I (Cost of Sales and Inventories)** policy (inventories not expected to be sold within 12 months are classified in *Other noncurrent assets*):

- Noncurrent inventories (not expected to be sold within one year) fell from **$4,568 million at December 31, 2023 to $2,663 million at December 31, 2024**, and Pfizer states the cause explicitly: *"The decrease from December 31, 2023 is primarily driven by a reduction in acquired Seagen inventory, inclusive of the acquisition accounting fair value step up"* (see Note 2A), adding: *"Based on our current estimates and assumptions, there are no recoverability issues for these amounts."* In other words, the acquired Seagen inventory recognized at fair value (including the step-up) was drawn down/sold through cost of sales in 2024 — consistent with Seagen's acquisition-date inventory of $1.1 billion current and $2.1 billion noncurrent (as adjusted) and with the $1.9 billion of Seagen inventory step-up amortization recorded in 2024 cost of sales. This release of noncurrent inventory is a source of operating cash flow in 2024, embedded in the favorable swing in "Other assets" (−$663 million in 2023 to +$3,380 million in 2024).
- **Offsetting within inventories:** *current* inventories actually **increased**, from $10,189 million to $10,851 million, which Pfizer attributes to *"higher inventory levels for certain products mainly due to changes in net market demand, network strategy and new product launches."* That build is a use of cash in the "Inventories" line (−$854 million in 2024 vs. −$1,169 million in 2023) and partly offsets the benefit from the noncurrent inventory release.

## Other timing items

Beyond the two the 10-K calls out, the ordinary-course timing of receipts and payments also moved against 2024 operating cash flow in the statement of cash flows: trade accounts payable (−$1,023 million in 2024 vs. −$300 million in 2023, reflecting the decline in BioNTech Comirnaty gross-profit-split payables from $2.0 billion to $1.3 billion), other liabilities (−$3,115 million), other tax accounts, net (−$1,345 million), and trade accounts receivable (−$109 million), partly offset by the favorable "Other assets" movement noted above.

**Net effect:** operating cash flow rose $4.0 billion to $12.7 billion — chiefly because 2024 earnings adjusted for non-cash items were much higher (no repeat of the $6.2 billion non-cash COVID-19 inventory write-off, higher revenue, lower cost of sales) and because the Seagen noncurrent inventory step-up unwound, partly offset by the drawdown of Comirnaty/Paxlovid advance payments, the build in current inventory, and other ordinary-course payment timing.

Its cash-requirements tables (MD&A Capital Resources) list only debt, interest, pension, purchase obligations, and 737 MAX concessions.
- **Berkshire Hathaway** — Note 19 (Income taxes) reports $90.2B of income tax liabilities, but only the indefinite-reinvestment statement ("We have not established deferred income taxes on accumulated undistributed earnings of certain foreign subsidiaries... Generally, no U.S. federal income taxes will be imposed on future distributions of foreign earnings"). No transition-tax amount.
- **ExxonMobil** — Note 19 (Income and Other Taxes) and the TAXES section of MD&A cover the 31% effective rate and $40.6B total taxes, with no transition-tax payable. Current "Income taxes payable" is only $1,601M.
- **Boeing** — Note 4 refers to the liability only in general terms: "The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) one-time repatriation tax and Global Intangible Low Tax Income liabilities effectively taxed the undistributed earnings previously deferred from U.S. income taxes." No remaining amount; "Income taxes payable" in accrued liabilities is just $5M.
